pixels-are-free-frames-are-expensive:
When I started building LiveWall, I assumed the expensive knob was resolution. It's the intuition everyone has: a 4K wallpaper must cost more than a 720p one. So I went to measure it before tuning anything, on an M3 Pro, against the real playback path, changing one variable at a time.

The intuition was wrong, and the way it was wrong is the most useful thing I learned on the project.

What the numbers said

Same clip, same code path. Resolution climbs 7.4× from the first row to the fourth:

  • 1280×720, 1.4 Mbps, 8-bit — 15 MB, 3.00% CPU
  • 1920×1080, 3.1 Mbps, 8-bit — 16 MB, 3.14% CPU
  • 1920×1080, 6.8 Mbps, 8-bit — 18 MB, 2.74% CPU
  • 3492×1964, 10 Mbps, 8-bit — 18 MB, 3.44% CPU
  • 1920×1080, 5.6 Mbps, 10-bit — 18 MB, 2.92% CPU
  • 1920×1080, 6.8 Mbps, 60 fps — 19 MB, 7.78% CPU

Seven times the pixels moves CPU from 3.00% to 3.44%, which is close to noise. Ten-bit colour is free. Nearly five times the bitrate is free. Then frame rate doubles and the cost lands at 7.78% — more than double, from the one change that doesn't touch pixel count at all.

Why

Hardware video decode is fixed-function silicon. It is flat in frame size: a 4K frame and a 720p frame both go through a dedicated block that the CPU is barely involved in. Once you accept that, the only cost left is your own program's per-frame pump — pulling a decoded frame, handing it to the compositor, and going back to sleep.

That work scales with frames per second and nothing else. Resolution, bit depth, and bitrate are the decoder's problem, and the decoder is not paying with your CPU budget.

So the shape of the cost curve isn't "how much data" — it's "how many times per second does my code have to wake up and do something."

What it changed

Once the measurement said that, the presets wrote themselves. LiveWall spends freely on resolution, bit depth and bitrate, because those are things the user can see and the machine doesn't charge for. It is aggressively frugal with frame rate, because that is the one axis where every step is paid for in CPU.

It also settled a design decision I'd been going back and forth on. When the wallpaper isn't visible, the obvious move is to slow the tick rate down rather than stop. But because the decode path pulls exactly one frame per tick over B-frame-free assets, halving the tick rate doesn't halve the cost — it plays the clip in slow motion. There is no cheap middle setting. So every stop condition in the app is a hard stop: the decoder and its session are destroyed, the last frame stays composited by the window server at zero cost, and playback resumes from the saved timestamp when you can see it again.

The general lesson

I nearly shipped a set of presets built on an assumption I'd never checked, and they would have been wrong in the specific direction of making the app look worse for no saving — lower resolution, same CPU.

The measurement took an afternoon. The script that produces those numbers is in the repo (tools/measure.sh), because a result like this is only worth anything if someone else can re-run it and tell me I'm wrong.
blocking-the-shape-of-a-number:
Every call blocker I tried wanted an exact number. You get a spam call, you block it, and you feel like you've done something. Then the next call comes from a number one digit away.

That asymmetry is the whole problem. Blocking an exact number costs the spammer nothing — they rotate through ranges, spoof prefixes, and burn a new line per call. You are playing a game where each of your moves removes one number from an effectively infinite pool. You cannot win it by adding rows to a list.

Block the shape instead

Globber is named after glob patterns, because that's the fix. You don't describe the number that called you; you describe the kind of number you never want to hear from:

+1 800 555 ****     →  block the whole 555 block
1900*               →  kill premium-rate prefixes
*0000               →  drop sequential robo-dialers

One rule retires an entire range. The pool stops being infinite, because you're no longer enumerating members of it — you're describing its boundary. Rules match by exact, starts-with, contains, ends-with, or regex, so the same mechanism covers "this one specific nuisance" and "every premium-rate line in the country."

Screening beats blocking

The other half is when it happens. Android's CallScreeningService hands your app each incoming call before the phone rings, and lets you reject it outright. The call never reaches the UI, never lights the screen, never makes a sound. It lands in a log you can review later if you want to.

This is a meaningfully different experience from an app that answers-and-hangs-up after the fact. Nothing interrupts you. The interruption is the thing you were trying to eliminate, so intercepting the call one layer earlier is most of the value.

The permission you don't grant

Globber has no INTERNET permission.

That isn't a privacy-policy promise, it's a manifest fact. Rule matching is string work against the incoming number; the block log is a local Room database. There is no step in that flow that needs a network, so the app doesn't request one — and an Android app without INTERNET cannot phone home, whatever its developer later decides.

It asks for two permissions, both optional in practice: READ_CONTACTS, to let known contacts through regardless of your rules, and POST_NOTIFICATIONS, to tell you a call was blocked. That's it. No analytics, no ads, and nothing to sell, because there's no pipe to sell it through.

I find this a more honest way to make a privacy claim than a paragraph in a policy document. Don't ask me to trust your intentions — show me you removed the capability.

Stack

Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, Room for rule and log persistence, CallScreeningService for the interception. minSdk 29, targetSdk 35. MIT licensed, signed APKs on GitHub Releases.
a-clock-that-reaches-out:
You sit down to work, blink, and three hours are gone. Meetings missed, breaks skipped, the day eaten. If that's never happened to you, this post is about a problem you don't have.

The frustrating part is that the fix seems obvious — look at a clock. But a clock is a pull interface. It sits there and waits to be read, which means it only works if you remember to read it. And remembering is precisely the faculty that goes offline when you're absorbed in something. The tool assumes the capability whose absence is the problem.

Push, not pull

Glint inverts that. Instead of waiting to be checked, it reaches out:

  • A warm amber → red wash builds over the final 10 seconds of a minute — a calm peripheral-vision signal that a change is coming.
  • A teal burst flashes the whole card when the minute rolls over.
  • A bigger orange → magenta burst and a double chime marks every hour.
  • At an interval you pick — 15, 25, 30 or 60 minutes — a violet blink and a triple chime: a deliberate tap on the shoulder.

You don't have to look. You feel time moving in your peripheral vision, and the information arrives whether or not you remembered to want it.

It floats above every window and every Space, PiP-style, so there's no "bring the clock forward" step to forget either. It ticks and tocks on alternating seconds — all of the audio synthesized in code, no bundled sound files.

Numbers are the wrong output

The part that surprised me was that showing the time is often not the useful thing.

Time Timer's research finds that a visual, number-free depiction of remaining time improves self-regulation and lowers anxiety. Reading "3:47" requires you to subtract from a target you also have to remember. Seeing a disk that's a third full requires nothing — it's a quantity, not a calculation.

So Glint can show a shrinking ring around the card, or become a faithful Time Timer dial: red disk depleting toward zero, a 0–55 minute ring, tick marks, a pointer hand. There's a display mode that hides the digits entirely. For time-blind users that's often the mode that works, which is a strange thing to discover about a clock.

There's a Calm Mode too, which swaps the alarm-style bursts for gentle depletion. An interruption that raises your heart rate solves one problem by creating another.

Small details that decide whether it stays installed

An always-on-top ticking clock is one bad edge case away from being uninstalled:

  • Auto-mute in calls. It silences the ticking while your mic is in use, so it never leaks into a meeting. That reads device state only — no microphone permission.
  • LSUIElement agent app. No Dock icon, no app switcher clutter. It's furniture, not an app you open.
  • Everything is remembered. 24-hour clock, three sizes, three flash intensities, position on screen, launch at login.

Pure Swift 6, AppKit and SwiftUI, no dependencies. macOS 13+. MIT licensed.
the-server-was-never-necessary:
Every online file converter works the same way. You pick a file. It uploads to a server you know nothing about. Something happens. You download the result.

For a holiday video or a folder of screenshots, look at what that trade actually is: to change a container format, you hand a copy of your file to a stranger's machine and take on faith what happens to it after. You also wait for the upload, and accept whatever size cap their bandwidth bill imposes.

None of that is inherent to converting a file. It's inherent to someone else's CPU doing it.

The premise

FFmpeg compiles to WebAssembly. ffmpeg.wasm is the real encoder — the same libx264, libvpx, libwebp — running in the browser tab.

So the file never moves. It's read from disk locally, converted locally, written back locally. There's no upload wait because there's no upload. There's no size limit because nobody is paying for the bandwidth. And the privacy question stops needing an answer, because there's nothing to answer for.

That's the converter I've been building.

If it's local, it should work with the wifi off

Here's the part I find most interesting, because it's the honest test of the claim.

If conversion genuinely happens on your machine, the app has no reason to need the network after the first visit. A converter that still breaks when the connection drops would be quietly admitting the work wasn't as local as advertised.

So it's installable and fully offline. A service worker precaches the app shell on install and drops superseded caches on activate. The fetch handler splits by request type, deliberately:

// Navigations: network-first, so HTML stays fresh online
// and falls back to cache when it isn't.
if (request.mode === 'navigate') {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(request);
    if (response.ok) await runtimeCache.put(request, response.clone());
    return response;
  } catch {
    return (await runtimeCache.match(request))
        ?? (await staticCache.match('/'))
        ?? new Response('Offline. Please reconnect once to refresh cache.', { status: 503 });
  }
}

// Assets: cache-first, no round trip needed.
const cachedStatic = await staticCache.match(request);
if (cachedStatic) return cachedStatic;

Network-first for HTML means you get updates when you're online. Cache-first for assets means the heavy artefacts load instantly and don't need the network at all.

The detail that decides whether "offline" is real

A service worker that caches your JavaScript and CSS gives you an app shell that renders offline and then fails the moment someone presses Convert. That's worse than being honestly online-only, because it fails later and more confusingly.

What makes it real is where the WebAssembly core comes from:

const [{ FFmpeg }, { default: coreURL }, { default: wasmURL }] = await Promise.all([
  import('@ffmpeg/ffmpeg'),
  import('@ffmpeg/core?url'),
  import('@ffmpeg/core/wasm?url')
]);

Those are bundled same-origin assets, not a CDN URL. That single decision is what puts ffmpeg-core.wasm into the build output the service worker precaches — so an offline visit has the actual encoder sitting on disk, not a shell with a hole where the encoder should be.

I checked rather than assumed. On the deployed site the precache holds 16 entries, and two of them are ffmpeg-core.js and ffmpeg-core.wasm.

Loading it is also wrapped in a 120-second timeout with an abort signal, because a wasm core that never resolves is otherwise an infinite spinner with nothing to tell the user.

The tax you pay for this

Browser FFmpeg needs SharedArrayBuffer, and browsers only hand that to cross-origin-isolated pages. Which means every response has to carry:

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp

Miss them and everything looks fine — the page renders, the UI works — right up until FFmpeg refuses to load, with an error that doesn't obviously point at HTTP headers. It's the single most common reason a browser-side FFmpeg project stalls, and it costs you the ability to casually embed third-party resources, since require-corp means every cross-origin subresource needs explicit opt-in.

That's a real constraint, not a footnote. It's the price of the whole approach, and it's worth paying.

What this generalises to

The interesting thing isn't the converter. It's that a whole category of "upload it to our server" tools exist because of an assumption that stopped being true.

Image resizing, audio trimming, PDF merging, format conversion — none of these are compute problems a modern laptop can't handle. They became services because the browser couldn't do them, and they stayed services after the browser could, because nobody revisited it.

Every one of those is a candidate for the same treatment: no upload, no queue, no account, no privacy policy to read. Just the work, on the machine that already has the file.
making-a-call-ring:
Adding voice calling to a Flutter app looks like picking a package. It isn't. The package is the easy part — what takes the time is everything around the moment the phone is supposed to ring, and most of it happens outside your Dart code.

Notes from building calling for Celestial, a telecare platform where a care team and the people they support call each other constantly.

One product, three calling systems

The first thing that stops being a single integration is calling itself.

In-app calls run through ZEGOCLOUD, which covers four different shapes: one-on-one voice, one-on-one video, group voice, group video. The config isn't fixed — it's derived per call from the invitation data, keying off whether the call is flagged as video and whether there's more than one invitee.

Phone calls go through Twilio Voice, because sometimes you need to reach a person on an actual phone number rather than only inside the app.

They coexist. A support worker calls a user in-app; if that doesn't connect, they call their phone. Two entirely separate stacks, two sets of platform concerns, one product.

A call is not "started" and "ended"

The naive model is a call connects and then it hangs up. The real state space is much bigger, and every branch has a distinct UI consequence:

  • The callee never answered and it timed out
  • The caller cancelled before the callee picked up
  • The callee declined
  • The callee was busy on another call
  • The callee's device was offline when the invitation went out
  • The invitation succeeded but the callee's app was killed

That last group matters most, because they're indistinguishable to a naive implementation and completely different to the user. "They declined" and "their phone was off" produce the same non-answer, and showing the wrong one is a small betrayal of the user's trust in the app.

So the invitation handler enumerates all of it — outgoing timeout, cancel, decline, busy, accepted, sent, incoming timeout, incoming cancel — plus a separate stream for invitee state transitions, where offline, timeout and rejected are handled as three different things rather than one failure.

Ringing like a phone, not like a notification

An in-app call that arrives as a banner notification is a bad call app. You want it to take over the screen, ring, and be answerable from the lock screen — which means registering with the platform's own calling UI: CallKit on iOS, ConnectionService on Android.

Doing that properly pulls in a chain of things that have nothing to do with your feature code:

  • Custom ringtones and separate notification channels per platform.
  • A minimisable overlay, so answering a call doesn't trap the user on one screen — they can navigate the app while talking, with the call reduced to a floating window.
  • Persisted call state, because the app may be launched by the call. When a user taps accept on a system call screen, your app might be starting from nothing, and it needs to know which call it's joining.

That last one is why there's a typed storage bucket holding just the incoming call payload and the most recently accepted call notification ID. It exists because a call can outlive the process that received it.

Six permissions, not one

Everyone remembers the microphone. On Android the actual list, each checked and requested independently:

  • microphone
  • READ_PHONE_STATE
  • READ_PHONE_NUMBERS
  • CALL_PHONE
  • MANAGE_OWN_CALLS
  • background notification permission

They fail independently too, and they fail differently — some are a dialog, some are a settings screen, some are silently denied by the OEM. Treating this as "request permissions" rather than six separate states with six separate recovery paths is how you get an app that mysteriously doesn't ring on one manufacturer's phones.

When the fix is in the plugin

The part I want to be most concrete about, because it's the case where reading the plugin source was the only way through.

Twilio's VoIP push on iOS relies on PKPushRegistry. In the plugin, that registry was constructed in the plugin's init():

public override init() {
    voipRegistry = PKPushRegistry.init(queue: DispatchQueue.main)
    // …
    voipRegistry.delegate = self
    voipRegistry.desiredPushTypes = Set([PKPushType.voIP])
}

Which means iOS starts VoIP push registration the instant the plugin loads — before the app has an access token, before anyone has logged in, before there's any identity to register against.

The fix is to make registration lazy, and tie it to the moment the token actually arrives:

if flutterCall.method == "tokens" {
    guard let token = arguments["accessToken"] as? String else { return }
    self.accessToken = token

    // Initialize VoIP registry when token is set
    initializeVoIPRegistry()
    // …
}

voipRegistry becomes optional rather than eagerly constructed. While in there, the clients dictionary was an implicitly-unwrapped [String:String]! assigned in init — a crash waiting for the one path that reads it before assignment — so that became a plain dictionary with an empty default.

I also implemented the macOS plugin, which didn't exist, and brought the Android toolchain up to current Kotlin, AGP and compileSdk.

All of it lives in a fork, and the app depends on the fork by git URL. Which is the practical lesson: when a plugin's lifecycle assumptions don't match your app's, you are going to end up in its native source. Budget for that on any calling feature, because "just add the package" is not what the work looks like.

What I'd tell someone starting

Calling is not a feature you add, it's a subsystem you adopt. The Dart API is the smallest part of it. The time goes to native lifecycle, permission matrices, the full enumeration of ways a call can fail, and state that has to survive your process dying.

Plan for the plugin to be wrong somewhere. It probably is — and when the bug is in a lifecycle assumption, no amount of Dart on top of it will help.
a-foundation-not-a-template:
Start enough Flutter projects at one company and you notice the first week is always the same week. Wire up the HTTP client. Decide how errors are represented. Pick a storage wrapper. Set up logging. Write the responsive helpers. Copy the extensions you liked from the last project.

Everyone does it, everyone does it slightly differently, and a year later "our Flutter apps" have nothing in common but the language.

This is what feg_cli and its packages were built to fix at Fegno.

The tempting wrong answer

The obvious fix is a starter repository. Set one up, tell everyone to clone it, done.

It doesn't work, and the reason is worth being precise about: a template is a copy, and copies drift. The moment someone clones it, their project owns that code. Fix a bug in the network layer and you've fixed it in the template — every app already shipped still has it. Six months on, you have eight codebases that were identical once and now differ in ways nobody can enumerate.

The distinction I care about is direction of dependency. With a template, projects depend on a snapshot they took. With packages, projects depend on something that can still change. Only the second one lets you fix things centrally.

So the foundation ships as twelve versioned packages on pub.dev — feggy_core, feggy_network, feggy_storage, feggy_security, feggy_exception, feggy_logger, feggy_responsive, feggy_sizer, feggy_extensions, feggy_fast_network_image, feggy_updater — and a project takes only what it needs. A fix ships to every app through a version bump.

But scaffolding is still a copy

Here's the tension: not everything can be a package. The folder structure of a feature, the wiring in main.dart, the CI config — that's code that has to live in your repo. You can't pub add a directory layout.

That part is generation, and generation is where a CLI earns its place:

dart pub global activate feg_cli

feg_cli create app       # scaffold an application
feg_cli create feature   # scaffold a feature inside it

create app asks for a project name and organisation, then asks what kind of app this is — Basic, E-Commerce, or Social Media. Each is a different Mason brick pulled from a template repository at generation time.

Sourcing bricks from git rather than bundling them in the CLI is deliberate. It means updating a template doesn't require publishing a new CLI version, and the templates evolve at the speed the team learns things rather than the speed of a release cycle.

So the split is: anything that can be a dependency is a package; anything that must be your code is generated. Packages for logic that should stay central, generation for structure that must be local.

The unglamorous commands are the useful ones

feg_cli also does two things that sound trivial and are not:

feg_cli change app_name
feg_cli change package_name

Renaming a Flutter app is a genuinely annoying task. The display name lives in AndroidManifest.xml and in iOS plist files. The package identifier is worse — it's in the manifest, in Gradle config, in the directory structure of the Kotlin sources, in the Xcode project. Miss one and you get a build that fails somewhere unhelpful, or worse, succeeds and ships wrong.

The manifest rewrite alone needs a regex that tolerates escaped quotes inside an attribute value:

line.replaceAll(
  RegExp(r'android:label="[^"]*(\\\"[^"]*)*"'),
  'android:label="$name"',
);

That's the kind of thing everyone solves badly, once, under time pressure, and then never looks at again. Solving it properly one time and putting it behind a command is a better use of an afternoon than any amount of architecture diagramming.

What actually changed

The measurable win is the first week — a new app starts with the fundamentals already in place.

The win I'd defend more strongly is consistency. When every app reaches for the same logger, the same exception types and the same storage interface, a developer moving between projects is productive immediately, because there's nothing project-specific to learn first. Onboarding stops being "let me explain how this one works."

And it makes the org's improvements compound. Someone hardening feggy_security improves every app that upgrades. Under the template model, that same work improves exactly one repository and slowly rots in the others.

That's the whole argument for packages over copies, and it's why the packaging decision mattered more than any code inside the packages.
